parakeet: People often assume there's one big moment that makes somebody leave their faith. A debate you watched, a book you read, a tragedy that shakes you to your core. It came through something far more personal. It came in hospital rooms with my heart racing as doctors fought to bring my children into the world. It came in late-night conversations at the edge of a child's bed when curiosity left me with no choice but to answer honestly. It came in the quiet but heavy responsibility of realizing I could either hand my kids the same prepackaged beliefs I grew up with, or I could give them the freedom to think for themselves. The secret catalyst to my deconversion wasn't doubt alone. It wasn't even disappointment in religion. It was fatherhood. Becoming a parent forced me to confront every crack in my theology. Every birth, every question, every promise to be honest with my children pulled me further away from faith and deeper into truth. All four of my children came into this world through C-sections. That wasn't what I imagined when I thought about fatherhood. In my mind, childbirth was supposed to be this natural, beautiful process, maybe even a sacred one. But from the very beginning, it was anything but predictable or smooth. Each birth was surrounded by danger. Each time I was reminded that life is fragile, that survival is never guaranteed. I can still remember sitting in that hospital room, heart pounding, praying prayers I wasn't even sure would reach anywhere, watching as doctors and nurses worked with precision, the beeping machines, the surgical masks, the tense looks on the staff's faces. They were the ones holding life and death in their hands. Not God, not faith, not my prayers. They were. And as each of my children finally cried out for the first time, I felt overwhelming gratitude, but not toward heaven, toward the humans in that room who used their training, their knowledge, and their courage to keep my wife and my children alive. Those moments carved something deep into me because I had been taught to see birth as evidence of God's design, a perfect plan unfolding. But what I saw didn't look perfect at all. If this was God's design, why did it require so much intervention? Why would the most natural, essential part of life, bringing children into the world, be so dangerous without surgery, medicine, and human ingenuity? If this was design, it looked flawed, it looked careless, and it put a crack right down the middle of my theology. The truth is, those experiences forced me to admit something I had avoided for years. The stories I'd been told about God's providence did not match reality. In sermons, I heard God provides. In delivery rooms, I saw how much we depended on science, on research, and on human creativity. And here's what hit me hardest. If not for those doctors, if not for those tools and procedures, my children wouldn't be here. Looking back, I realized those hospital rooms became sacred spaces for me, not because of God's presence, but because they showed me the truth. They exposed the gap between what I was told to believe and what I actually saw with my own eyes. And once you see that gap, you can't unsee it. One of the biggest shifts that came with fatherhood was realizing that I couldn't coast. I couldn't just fall back on the idea that God had written my children's future in some cosmic script, and my job was simply to pray, obey, and hope for the best. That idea that our purpose is already pre-written was one of the biggest lies that I started to resent. Because when it came to raising my kids, I knew deep down I couldn't afford to be passive. Their lives couldn't be left up to divine mystery. They needed a father who was awake, intentional, and deliberate. Religion had trained me to think in terms of destiny. God has a plan for your life. But the more I looked at my children, the more hollow that sounded. If their lives were already mapped out, what did my responsibility as a parent even matter? Was I just supposed to stand back and let God's will unfold? That didn't sit right with me. Fatherhood exposed how lazy that thinking was and why so many families are in such a bad place now. The truth was raising children demanded purpose, not the kind that's handed down from a pulpit, but the kind that's built brick by brick in the choices you make every single day and how you engage those consequences. Purpose meant deciding how I would discipline, how I would nurture, how I would shape an environment where curiosity wasn't punished, but encouraged. Purpose meant staying up late for conversations, showing up for games and recitals, modeling integrity in the way that I treated their mother, the way that I handled stress, and even the way that I talked about people who disagreed with me. And the more I leaned into that, the more I started to see purpose differently. It wasn't this one size fits all calling stamped on us from heaven. It was something I had to create, something I had to live into with intention. Being a parent on purpose taught me that meaning isn't found, it's made. In many ways, fatherhood reprogrammed me. It broke down my dependence on the idea of divine design and replaced it with a hunger for intentional living. It forced me to ask if I reject non-intentional purpose for my children, why would I keep accepting it for myself? When my oldest son started talking and asking questions, it was like watching a mirror of my younger self. He had this brilliant, restless mind, curious about everything, constantly pulling on threads, trying to make sense of the world around him. And in him, I saw both the kid I used to be and the adult I needed to become. When I was his age, I craved that kind of intellectual support. I wanted someone who wouldn't just hand me pre-packaged answers or shut me down with just have faith. But instead, I learned early on that curiosity was dangerous, that too many questions could get you labeled, rebellious, doubtful, or sinful. I experienced that firsthand. Countless people would warn my mother that I was too inquisitive and the devil would use it against me. I carried that wound for years. So when my son started asking the same types of questions I had once asked, I made myself a promise. I wasn't going to do to him what had been done to me. Let me tell you, kids don't let you get away with easy answers. When he asked me something, I could feel the weight of it because if I fed him the same old religious clichés, he would see right through it. He deserved honesty. He deserved respect. He deserved a father who wasn't afraid to admit when something didn't make sense. Those conversations became a kind of accountability for me. I realized I couldn't keep living with one foot in faith and one foot in doubt.
